finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.assumptions: The 'country' input is attacker-controlled and directly used in constructing a URL that is fetched using libcurl. If the server at 'https://www.officeholidays.com' is vulnerable to path traversal or other attacks, this could lead to unintended behavior.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the URL construction on line 22 merely concatenates user input into a string passed to libcurl. libcurl performs an HTTP(S) request; it does not invoke a shell or execute the URL as a command. Therefore the input cannot be used to inject OS commands. No sanitization is required for this sink, and the code does not call any system or exec family functions. The reported trigger would only result in a malformed URL, not a command execution.

finding.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
finding.assumptions: The HTML content fetched from the URL is directly parsed and displayed without proper sanitization. If the fetched content contains malicious scripts, they could be executed in the client's browser.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the sink xmlNodeGetContent retrieves the *text content* of an XML node, not raw HTML markup. The extracted strings (date and holiday) are printed to stdout (lines 119‑124) rather than injected into a browser DOM. Therefore even if the fetched HTML contains a <script> element, its contents would be treated as plain text and displayed in the console, not executed. No XSS path exists.

finding.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
finding.trigger: response contains special characters that could be used in OS command injection
finding.assumptions: The HTML content fetched from the URL is directly parsed and used in constructing file paths or other OS commands. If the fetched content contains special characters, they could be used to inject malicious commands.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked the code for any OS command execution (e.g., system(), exec(), popen(), or similar). No such calls are present. The reported sink xmlNodeGetContent is used only to extract text from HTML nodes and store it in a vector; it does not construct or execute any command. Therefore, there is no path from the untrusted source 'response' to an OS command execution. The lines 75-76 merely convert node content to std::string and push it into a vector, which is safe. No neutralisation checks are required because the operation is not a command execution.

finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.assumptions: The HTML content fetched from the URL is directly parsed and used in constructing OS commands. If the fetched content contains malicious commands, they could be executed on the server.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked the code for any invocation of OS command execution functions such as system(), exec(), spawn, or similar. The only operations performed on the untrusted response are parsing with libxml2 (htmlReadDoc) and extracting node contents via xmlNodeGetContent. No command execution occurs, so the reported sink does not lead to OS command injection.
